blocks.text: **Anatomical Dead Space Volume** is the volume of air that occupies the conducting zone of the airways and does not participate in the gaseous exchange.
**Key Points:** This volume can vary depending on the body weight or the size of the lung of the person.
**Measurement:** Anatomical dead space volume is calculated as 2.2 multiplied by the body weight (kg) of the person.

Increased volume of this anatomical dead space will be seen in any condition where there is dilation of the conduction zone, or if there is an increased length of this conducting zone. Any kind of bronchodilation experienced by a person will increase the anatomical dead space volume because bronchus and bronchioles will be dilated, which will entrap more dead volume.
If general anesthesia is given to a person, there will be a loss of bronchial tone, and dilation will be more, which will be more anatomical dead space. (Option A).

In inspiration the length of the anatomical dead space zone is increasing, hence dead space volume will also increase. Extension of the neck and protrusion of the jaw, all done during anesthesia will result in increased anatomical dead space.

Velocity is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. In the respiratory system, consider the cross-sectional area of different segments like a cross-section of the trachea, both the bronchus and bronchioles, etc, The total cross-sectional area is minimum at division number 3. Hence velocity is highest.
Velocity will be maximum at division number 3 and then velocity progressively decreases towards the alveoli, and minimum velocity is seen at the level of alveoli.

items.text: **Alveoli(Option A):** The alveoli have the largest total cross-sectional area, leading to minimal airflow velocity and predominantly laminar flow.
**Terminal bronchioles(Option C):** Terminal bronchioles have a larger cumulative cross-sectional area than the trachea, leading to lower airflow velocity and smoother flow
**Respiratory bronchioles (Option D):** Respiratory bronchioles, being part of the gas exchange zone, have an even greater cross-sectional area, causing minimal velocity and mostly laminar flow.

blocks.text: The medium to large-size bronchi, specifically the lobar and segmental bronchi, are the site of maximum resistance to airflow. This is because these bronchi have a relatively larger radius but are fewer in number, resulting in higher individual resistance. According to Poiseuille's law, resistance to airflow (R) is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius (r) of the airway.
**Resistance:** R = 8ηL/πr 4
Therefore, small changes in the radius result in significant changes in resistance. Despite the smaller radius of the bronchioles, their parallel arrangement results in a lower total resistance.

items.text: The upper airways (pharynx and larynx) also contribute significantly to airflow resistance but less than medium to large-sized bronchi.(Option D)
Only about 20% of the resistance occurs at the level of the small airways. (Option B)
Alveoli have a large cross-sectional area which significantly reduces the resistance according to Poiseuille’s law. Option C)
Clara cells, also known as club cells, are non-ciliated, dome-shaped cells found in the bronchioles of the respiratory tract. (Option A ruled out)
They play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the bronchiolar epithelium by stabilising surfactant proteins that reduce surface tension. (Option B ruled out)
They are involved in detoxifying harmful substances through their enzymatic activity. (Option D ruled out)

blocks.text: They are not ciliated, differentiating them from other epithelial cells in the respiratory tract that do have cilia, such as the pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelial cells found in the trachea and larger bronchi.

The epithelial lining of trachea and large bronchi are composed of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. Ciliated epithelium is present at the level of the trachea, bronchus, and bronchioles. Cartilaginous rings are present up to the bronchi. Smooth muscles are present up to respiratory bronchioles (bronchial tone). (Option D ruled out)

blocks.text: Closing Volume (CV)

**Definition:** Closing Volume (CV) is the lung volume at which small airways begin to close during expiration, particularly in the dependent parts of the lungs. (Option A ruled out) CV = Closing capacity - Residual volume.

**Mechanism:** During expiration, as lung volume decreases, pleural pressure becomes less negative. At the closing volume, airway pressure drops below pleural pressure, causing small airways to close.
**Measurement:** Single-Breath Nitrogen Washout Test: This test measures CV by observing the washout of nitrogen from the lungs during a single breath.
**Clinical Implications:** Increased CV: Indicates small airway dysfunction and can be seen in: (Option D ruled out)

items.text: **Ageing:** Decreased elastic recoil and increased lung compliance.
**Obstructive Lung Diseases:** COPD and asthma.
**Obesity and Pregnancy:** Reduced lung volumes and diaphragmatic changes.
**Smoking:** Indicates early small airway dysfunction.

blocks.text: Closing Capacity (CC)
**Definition:** Closing Capacity (CC) is the lung volume at which the basal alveoli begin to close off during expiration. It is the sum of the closing and residual volumes (CC = CV + RV).

**Mechanism:** During forceful expiration, the volume at which only the basal alveoli are closed off is known as closing capacity. Further expiration will eventually lead to all alveoli being closed off, reaching the residual volume.

**Clinical Implications:** Ageing: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is greater than CC in a normal adult. By around 66 years of age, FRC is nearly equal to CC, indicating that CC increases gradually with age.
**Pathological Implications:** If CC significantly exceeds FRC, it indicates highly collapsible lung diseases, such as hyaline membrane disease.
**Measurement:** Single-Breath Nitrogen Washout Method (Fowler's) measures CC and anatomical dead space by observing nitrogen washout during a single breath. (Option B ruled out)

Dynamic compression of the airways occurs primarily during the late phase of forceful expiration when intrathoracic pressure (pleural pressure) exceeds airway pressure. This leads to airway narrowing or collapse, particularly in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), with increased resistance and decreased elastic recoil.
**Mechanism:** During forceful expiration, elastic tissues in the alveoli help in passive expiration by recoiling inward.

As air moves through the bronchi and bronchioles, airway resistance causes the pressure to drop. An external force from the chest wall also acts on the bronchi and bronchioles. At the end of expiration, the pressure inside the bronchioles equals the external pressure, known as the equal pressure point.

items.text: Dynamic compression does not occur during the early expiration phase when the lung volume is still relatively high; the surrounding lung tissue generally supports the airways well. (Option A)
Dynamic compression is not associated with functional residual capacity (FRC) but occurs later when airway and pleural pressures interact. (Option B)
When reaching the residual volume (RV) by the end of expiration, dynamic compression is less of a concern, as the airflow has largely ceased. (Option D)

blocks.text: A residual volume of 1200 ml is normal for a healthy 35-year-old male. Residual volume remains stable unless there is a pathological condition affecting lung function, and it helps differentiate between obstructive and restrictive lung diseases:

items.text: Obstructive lung diseases (e.g., COPD) increase residual volume due to air trapping.
Restrictive lung diseases (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis) decrease residual volume due to reduced lung compliance.

blocks.text: Additionally, residual volume can differentiate between types of restrictive lung diseases:
**Parenchymal restrictive lung disease (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis)** shows highly reduced residual volume due to stiff and scarred lung tissue.

**Extra-parenchymal restrictive lung disease (e.g., neuromuscular diseases, chest wall deformities)** may show normal or slightly reduced residual volume, as the issue is outside the lung tissue, affecting breathing mechanics rather than the lung parenchyma.
Key parameters of pulmonary function tests:
Spirometry

items.text: **Forced Vital Capacity (FVC):** Total air exhaled forcefully after deep breath. Approximately 4-6 liters (depending on age, sex, height, and weight)
**Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 Second (FEV 1):** Air exhaled in the first second of the FVC manoeuvre. Approximately 80% of FVC
**FEV 1 /FVC Ratio:** Percentage of FVC exhaled in the first second. Approximately 70-80%
**Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF):** Maximum speed of expiration. Varies by age, sex, and height (e.g., 400-600 L/min for adults)

blocks.text: Lung Volumes

items.text: **Total Lung Capacity (TLC):** The total volume of air in the lungs after maximal inhalation Approximately 6-8 liters
**Residual Volume (RV):** Air remaining in the lungs after maximal exhalation Approximately 1.2-1.5 litres
**Vital Capacity (VC):** Air that can be exhaled after maximal inhalation (FVC minus RV) Approximately 4-5 liters
**Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV):** Additional air inhaled after normal inhalation Approximately 2-3 liters
**Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV):** Additional air exhaled after normal exhalation Approximately 1-1.5 liters

blocks.text: **Diffusing Capacity (DLCO):** Lung’s ability to transfer gases (e.g., CO) Approximately 20-30 mL/min/mmHg
The other options (A, B, and D) are also within normal ranges for healthy adults but are less specific to routine findings in pulmonary function tests compared to residual volume.
Emphysema is an obstructive lung disease. Increased Residual Volume and Total Lung Capacity are the findings in obstructive lung disease.

FEV is less than 80% of TLC

Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) is the maximum flow velocity in litres per minute with air being forced out of the lungs.(Option A)
PEFR is recorded by using the peak-flow meter.(Option B)
The normal value of PEFR is 400 to 600 L/min or 6 to 10 L/s.(Option C)

blocks.text: PEFR is an index of patency of airways.

**Maximum Mid-expiratory Flow Rate (MMEFR):** Maximum flow achieved during the middle third of the total expired volume. Forced expiratory flow at 25% to 75% of the lung volume. Indicates the patency of small airways.
More sensitive marker of airway disease (particularly for the obstruction of smaller-sized airways) than traditional parameters like FEV1, FEV1/FVC ratio, or PEFR.
**PEFR (Option A)** – Less sensitive as it reflects large airway function and can remain normal in early small airway disease.
**FEV1 (Option B):** Commonly used but detects moderate-to-severe airway obstruction, making it less sensitive for early disease.
**FEV1/FVC Ratio (Option C):** Helps diagnose obstructive lung diseases, but may not detect early small airway dysfunction as well as MMEFR.

blocks.text: FEV1/FVC of this person is 80%
**FEV1 (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second):** Volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled in the first second of expiration.
**FVC (Forced Vital Capacity):** Total volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after taking a deep inhalation.
Here, FEV1 = 4L FVC = 5L FEV1/FVC ratio = (FEV1/FVC) × 100 = (4/5) × 100 = 80%
**Interpretation of Values:**

items.text: **Normal Ratio (70%-80% or higher):** Indicates normal lung function.
**Low Ratio (<70%):** Suggests obstructive lung disease.
**Normal or High Ratio with Reduced Volumes:** Suggests restrictive lung disease.
